dedupe_keys.name: multi hazard location based early warning demonstration in sogn og fjordane clim atic

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes a demonstration, in 2008-2011 under the EU Northern Periphery Programme project Clim-ATIC, of a multi-hazard population warning system in Sogn og Fjordane county, western Norway, tested in Aurland municipality, which faces avalanches, rock slides, floods and storm surges and receives many tourists. The system sends SMS and spoken messages to all fixed and mobile phones within a set distance of a hazard, with social media as a supplement, and was tested with a sample warning, a survey and data analysis. Sharing one system across natural and man-made hazards spreads its cost, and running it from Alarmsentralen, the county's inter-municipal emergency centre staffed around the clock, would need little extra cost. A reference group met four times with the County Governor, Western Norway Research Institute, the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate, the Public Roads Administration, Telenor, the telecoms regulator, NRK and E-CO hydropower. The project cost about 105,145 euros, shared by the County Governor and the NPP. The page, published in 2014 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML on the Climate-ADAPT portal. Caveats: the system was not adopted because of budget limits and confidentiality rules on sharing telecom location data. It illustrates cross-sector emergency response and evacuation warning for roads, dams and communities under multiple hazards and climate adaptation; related records are the Global Disaster Alert and Coordination System and the Engadin Protect Bio case study.

outcomes: The test showed that location-based phone warnings can be issued cost-effectively through existing emergency structures, but the system was not implemented because of budget and legal barriers.
